subject: zoology
question_text: Explain the pathogenicity of Wuchereria bancrofti in man.

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya Junior Fastrack zoology section (book p.67, Star Q 186). Zoology holds only ONE source book — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only, and no zoology board paper is in the corpus — so the two-book union check and the back-test are both structurally impossible for this card; 'not checked' does NOT mean 'checked and clean'. The mark split is a claim until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

steps.label: The worm and its place
lines: Wuchereria bancrofti is commonly called the
filarial worm.
The adult worms live coiled in the lymph vessels
of man, so every effect of this parasite falls
on the lymphatic system.
steps.why: Every symptom in this answer comes from a blocked or inflamed lymph vessel, so naming the habitat first makes the rest of the answer follow on its own.
common_mistakes: Writing that the worm lives in the blood vessels. The adult lives in the lymph vessels.
Confusing the adult with the microfilaria. The microfilaria is the larva in the blood.
steps.memory_tip: Adults in the lymph vessels, so the damage is lymphatic from start to finish.
steps.margin_note: Two lines: the common name and the place it lives.

steps.label: Light infection
lines: A light infection causes filarial fever,
headache and depression.
These are the first signs and they can be
mistaken for an ordinary fever.
steps.why: The disease is graded by the number of worms, so the answer separates a light infection from a heavy one instead of describing one single illness.
common_mistakes: Skipping the light infection and going straight to elephantiasis.
Writing that a light infection causes swelling. Swelling belongs to a heavy infection.
steps.memory_tip: Few worms, few signs: fever, headache and depression only.
steps.margin_note: One short block. Do not spend more than two lines here.

steps.label: Heavy infection
lines: A heavy infection inflames the lymph vessels and
the lymph glands. Inflammation of the lymph
vessels is called lymphangitis and inflammation
of the lymph glands is called lymphadenitis.
The dead worms clog the lymph vessels and the
lymph glands, so the lymph cannot drain and the
affected part swells.
steps.why: The blockage is what turns the disease from a fever into a swelling, and the two named inflammations are the terms this chapter asks for again as a separate question.
common_mistakes: Swapping the two terms. Lymphangitis is the vessels and lymphadenitis is the glands.
Writing that the living worms block the vessels. The dead worms clog them.
steps.memory_tip: Vessels and glands both inflame, then dead worms block them and the lymph cannot drain.
steps.margin_note: Two lines: the two named inflammations, then the blockage and the swelling.

steps.label: Elephantiasis
lines: Fibrous tissue collects near the swollen parts.
The sweat glands break down and the skin becomes
thick and rough.
This final condition is called elephantiasis.
The legs, the arms, the scrotum and the breasts
are the parts usually affected.
steps.why: Elephantiasis is the end of the chain, not a separate disease, so it is written last and is described by the three changes that produce it.
common_mistakes: Writing that elephantiasis appears at once. It is the end of a long, heavy infection.
Naming the condition without describing the fibrous tissue and the rough skin.
steps.memory_tip: Block, swell, harden: the swelling turns fibrous and the skin turns rough.
steps.margin_note: Name the condition in the box, then three short lines. Closing mark.

insider_note: The answer is graded light to heavy to final, so keep the three stages separate — merging them loses two of the four marks.
